chats.title: Reviewers running code and citation skew

messages.text: I've been reviewing a lot of manuscripts lately and it bothers me that nobody actually runs the analysis code. I think peer reviewers should be expected to check the code and data, at least to the point of re-running the main figure. Is there any precedent for journals building reproducibility checks into the review stage itself rather than leaving it to post-publication?

There is some precedent. A few journals in economics, political science and computational fields employ data editors who re-run submitted replication packages before acceptance. Others ask reviewers to tick a checklist about code availability without requiring execution. The models differ in who does the work: volunteer reviewers, paid staff, or a dedicated reproducibility reviewer added to the panel. The main barriers reported are time cost, environment setup, and confidential or very large datasets. A staged approach, where a light check (does the code run, does it produce the headline numbers) is mandatory and a deep audit is optional, tends to be the most realistic starting point.

That staged idea makes sense. Related thing I keep noticing while doing literature reviews: the papers with clean positive results get cited constantly, while careful null results on the same question just sit there with two or three citations. I suspect citation bias toward positive findings is distorting what the field thinks is settled. How would I actually measure that rather than just complaining about it?

A common design is to assemble a set of studies addressing the same question, code each one as supportive or null based on its primary outcome, and then model citation counts while controlling for journal, publication year, sample size and author team size. Citation network analysis adds another layer: you can check whether later reviews and meta-analyses disproportionately cite the positive studies. Negative binomial regression is typical for count data. The tricky parts are coding the direction of results reliably, ideally with two independent coders, and handling the fact that positive studies may also be larger or better designed, which you'd want to adjust for.

I like the two-coder approach. I think I'll start with one well-defined question where there are maybe forty studies, so I can do it by hand before trying to automate any of it. Honestly both of these problems feel connected to me: if reviewers checked code, fewer shaky positive results would get through, and the citation skew would have less to feed on.

That's a reasonable framing and a manageable pilot. Forty studies is enough to see a pattern and small enough to code carefully. You might pre-register the coding rules and the regression model before collecting citation counts so the analysis can't drift toward the answer you expect. If you later want to link it to the reproducibility point, you could note which of those forty studies shared code and whether that is associated with citation rate, though causal claims would be hard to support.

I'm curious whether open commenting on preprints actually improves the final papers. My hunch is that public post-publication review catches real problems, but I've seen very few studies that compare the preprint version to the published version and ask whether the changes trace back to public comments. Has anyone done that systematically?

There's limited work on this. Some studies compare preprints to their published versions and find that changes are usually modest, mostly to wording and presentation rather than conclusions. Fewer studies link specific changes to specific public comments, because most preprints receive no comments at all, and comments on social media are scattered. A credible design would sample preprints that did receive substantive public comments, match them with similar preprints that received none, and code the differences between versions. Text diffing tools can help locate changes before manual coding.

The matched design is what I had in mind. One thing I could add: I built a small tool last year that flags duplicated or manipulated images in papers, things like reused western blot panels or cloned regions in microscopy images. I could run it over both preprint and published versions to see whether image problems flagged in public comments actually get fixed. Is that a sensible use of it?

That's a neat addition, because image issues are concrete and verifiable, unlike vague methodological critiques. You could measure three things: how often image problems exist in preprints, how often they're raised publicly, and how often they're corrected before journal publication. The main caveat is false positives; you'd want manual confirmation of every flag before counting it as a problem. It would also help to document your detector's precision and recall on a labeled set so readers trust the numbers.

I do have a labeled validation set from when I built it, and I've been sharing the detector with a couple of labs who asked. I'd happily make it available to anyone working on research integrity. I'll write up the validation numbers properly so the preprint study can cite them.

Writing up the validation separately is a good move; it gives the tool a citable reference and makes the preprint study cleaner. Consider releasing it with clear documentation of the image types it handles well and the ones it doesn't, plus a sample dataset. A short methods note describing the detection approach, thresholds, and known failure modes would make it much easier for other groups to adopt it and to interpret flags responsibly.

I'm drafting a short opinion piece arguing that review should include reproducibility checks. My view is that someone on the review panel should actually run the code and confirm the data match what's reported. A colleague pushed back that reviewers are already overloaded. Can you help me think through who should carry that burden?

A few options are worth laying out. Journals can hire data editors, which is reliable but costly. They can add a specialist reproducibility reviewer, often an early-career researcher who is paid or credited. They can require authors to supply containerized environments so checking is quick. Or they can use automated checks that confirm the code runs end to end and flag missing files. Many proposals combine author-side packaging with a dedicated checker, so the regular scientific reviewers aren't asked to do it on top of everything else.

A dedicated checker role feels right to me. The other angle I want in the piece is open review. If preprints are posted with code, then public commenters could also attempt reproduction, and that might spread the work around. I'm not sure whether open post-publication commenting on preprints actually leads to better papers though, or just more noise.

That uncertainty is fair. Open commenting has clear benefits when commenters have relevant expertise and when authors respond, but participation is low and uneven, and quality varies. Crowdsourced reproduction attempts have worked in a few high-profile cases, mostly where a result was surprising enough to attract attention. For an opinion piece, you could present open review as a complement: formal reproducibility checks guarantee a minimum standard, while public commenting provides extra scrutiny for papers that draw interest.

Good, that framing avoids overclaiming. I'll say formal reproducibility checks are the floor and open preprint review is a possible bonus whose value we still haven't measured well. Maybe I'll close by saying someone should actually study whether public comments change the final paper.

That's a strong closing because it turns an open question into a call for evidence. You could briefly sketch what such a study would look like, comparing preprints with and without substantive comments and tracking changes to methods or conclusions in the published version. Keeping the piece concrete like that tends to make opinion articles more persuasive to editors and readers.

chats.title: Null results citations and image flags

messages.text: I've been coding my citation dataset and the pattern is stark: in my pilot set, studies reporting a positive effect get roughly three times as many citations as null studies of similar size. I want to make sure I'm not fooling myself. What confounders should I worry about when claiming positive results are cited more than null results?

Key confounders include journal prestige, since positive studies may land in higher-visibility venues; publication date, as older papers accumulate more citations; sample size and design quality; author prominence; and whether the study was the first on the topic. Self-citation can inflate counts too. You could also check whether null studies are cited in a different way, for example only in passing within lists. Adjusting for venue and year in your model, plus a sensitivity analysis excluding self-citations, would address the most obvious concerns.

Venue is a big one, I'll add it. Here's a side question. I ran my image duplication detector over the same set of papers out of curiosity, and a few highly cited positive studies have flagged images. I built the tool myself, so I know its limits, but I'm wondering whether manipulated images could partly explain why some positive results look so clean.

It's an interesting hypothesis, but be careful with how you present it. Flags from an automated detector are leads, not findings, and a small number of cases can't explain a citation-wide pattern. If you pursue it, have independent people review each flag blind to citation count and result direction. Then you could test whether confirmed image problems are more common in positive studies than null ones. Any individual case should go through proper integrity channels rather than being named in a paper.

Agreed, I won't name anything. I'll treat it as an exploratory secondary analysis with blinded confirmation. And if other people doing citation or integrity work want to use the detector, I'm glad to share it; it's been sitting on my drive doing nothing most of the time.

That sounds like a responsible plan. Pre-specifying the secondary analysis and reporting it as exploratory will protect you from accusations of fishing. If you share the detector, a short usage guide explaining that flags require human review would help others use it carefully. You might also invite collaborators to contribute labeled examples, which would improve the tool's accuracy over time.

chats.title: Code checks, image tool, ecology RRs

messages.text: I've been invited to propose changes to how a small society journal runs review. My first suggestion is that reviewers, or a designated checker, should verify the code and data before acceptance. Second, I'd offer the image-duplication detector I built so the editorial office can screen submissions automatically. Does bundling those two sound coherent, or too much at once?

Bundling them is coherent because both are integrity checks that happen before publication, one for computational reproducibility and one for image integrity. The risk is editorial workload. You could propose that image screening run automatically at submission, with only flagged cases going to a human, while the code check happens later, only for papers likely to be accepted. Framing it as a pilot for one year with clear metrics, such as time per check and issues found, makes approval easier.

A one-year pilot is smart. The journal is mostly ecology, and I'm also tempted to suggest registered reports. I keep thinking ecology is a field where registered reports could help a lot, because field seasons are long and analysis choices get made after seeing messy data. But I'm unsure how they'd work when a study gets wrecked by a drought or a flood.

That's a real concern for ecology. Some journals handle it by allowing documented deviations: authors report what changed, why, and how the analysis adapted, and reviewers judge whether the deviations were justified. Contingency plans can also be written into the Stage 1 protocol, for instance alternative sites or analyses if sampling is disrupted. Long-term or multi-season studies may need interim reports. Being explicit that unforeseen environmental events won't automatically void acceptance would make ecologists more willing to try the format.

Contingency plans in the protocol is exactly the piece I was missing. So my proposal will be three parts: a code and data check, automated image screening with my tool, and a registered report track adapted for ecology field seasons.

That's a clear, well-scoped package. Consider ordering it by ease of adoption: image screening first since it's nearly automatic, then the code check pilot, then the registered report track, which needs editor training and author guidelines. Including a short paragraph on expected costs and a plan to evaluate each part after a year would give the board confidence that the changes are measured rather than experimental for their own sake.

chats.title: Do preprint comments fix citation bias

messages.text: I've been wondering whether open post-publication review on preprints could counteract citation bias. My worry is that positive results get cited more than null results, and public comments might be one place where people point to null studies that the authors ignored. Is that plausible, or am I connecting two unrelated things?

It's plausible as a mechanism, though probably weak in practice. Public commenters sometimes note missing references, including contradicting or null studies, and authors may add them in revision. But commenting rates are low, so the aggregate effect on citation patterns would be small. A testable version is narrower: among preprints that received substantive public comments, how often did the comments request additional citations, and were those citations disproportionately to null or contradicting work?

That narrower version is doable. I could code the comments for whether they ask for missing citations and whether those are null results. Then compare reference lists between the preprint and published version. If public review does nudge authors toward citing null findings, that would be a nice small result.

Yes, and it pairs well with your broader citation bias work. You'd need a way to classify the newly added references as positive, null or mixed, which could reuse your existing coding scheme. Be prepared for a small sample; you may need to pool across several preprint servers or disciplines. Even a descriptive finding, such as what fraction of comments request citations at all, would be informative.

I'll pool across servers. Part of me suspects the effect will be close to zero, but even a clear null would be worth publishing, which is kind of the whole point of my citation bias argument. If null results deserve to be cited, my own null result deserves to be written up properly too.

That's a nicely consistent stance. Pre-registering the analysis would make a null result more credible and harder to dismiss. You could also report an equivalence test to show the effect is reliably small rather than just not significant. Framing it that way demonstrates the kind of null reporting you're advocating for. It would also be worth stating in advance what effect size you would consider practically meaningful, so readers can judge the result against a clear benchmark.

I want to extend the image duplication detector I built. Right now it handles copied panels and rotated or flipped duplicates reasonably well, but it struggles with images that have been contrast-adjusted before reuse. Any suggestions for making it more robust to brightness and contrast changes without exploding the false positive rate?

A few approaches can help. Normalizing local contrast before comparison, for instance with histogram equalization on patches, reduces sensitivity to global adjustments. Feature descriptors based on gradients rather than raw intensity are more invariant to brightness shifts. You could also compare edge maps or structural similarity on normalized patches. To control false positives, require multiple matching keypoints with consistent geometric transforms, and calibrate thresholds on your labeled set including adjusted examples.

Gradient-based descriptors are worth a try. While I'm in tool-building mode, I've also been thinking about a second checker for statistical reporting errors: parsing reported test statistics and degrees of freedom, recomputing the p-value, and flagging inconsistencies. I know something like this exists, but I'd want it to handle more test types and messy PDF text.

That's a useful extension of existing approaches. The hard parts are text extraction from PDFs, where symbols and minus signs get mangled, and recognizing varied reporting formats. You'd want regex patterns for t, F, chi-square, z and correlation tests, plus handling for one-tailed tests and rounding. Flagging only gross inconsistencies, such as a reported significant p-value when the recomputed one isn't, keeps noise down. A validation set of hand-checked papers would be essential.

Good point about only flagging gross errors first. Long term I'd love to run both tools together on the same corpus, images and statistics, and see whether papers with one type of problem tend to have the other. For now I'll prioritize the contrast issue in the image tool since people are already using it.

That prioritization makes sense given existing users. Running both checks on the same corpus is an interesting idea, since co-occurrence of different error types could indicate general carelessness or something more serious, though you'd need careful framing. Releasing the improved image detector with a changelog and updated validation metrics will help current users understand what changed. A short note on known remaining failure modes would set expectations.

chats.title: Grant pitch: code review and citations

messages.text: I'm sketching a small funding proposal with two aims. Aim one: test whether asking reviewers to check code and data during peer review catches errors that would otherwise be published. Aim two: quantify how much more positive results are cited than null results in a few fields. Does that sound like one project or two awkwardly glued together?

It can read as one project if you frame it around a shared theme, such as how the publication system filters and amplifies findings. Aim one is about the filter, what review lets through; aim two is about amplification, what gets cited. A linking hypothesis helps, for example that results which would fail a reproducibility check are disproportionately positive and highly cited. Without a link, reviewers may see two separate studies.

The filter and amplification framing is great. For aim one I was planning a randomized design: some submissions get a standard review, others get an added reproducibility check where someone runs the code. Then we count errors found. My concern is getting journals to agree to randomize.

Journal buy-in is often the bottleneck. Options include partnering with one or two journals that already value transparency, randomizing only accepted papers to an extra post-acceptance check so outcomes aren't affected, or using a retrospective design where checkers re-run code from recently published papers. The post-acceptance version is the easiest sell, since it doesn't change editorial decisions but still measures how many errors standard review missed.

Post-acceptance randomization is much easier to pitch, I'll use that. Then for aim two I'll reuse my hand-coded citation dataset and expand it to three fields. If the papers that fail reproducibility checks also turn out to be the highly cited positive ones, that would tie everything together nicely.

That's a coherent plan. Make sure the power calculation for aim one is realistic, since error rates may be low and you'll need enough papers. For aim two, specify in advance how you'll define fields and classify results. A short section on expected outcomes under different scenarios, including null findings, would show reviewers the project is informative regardless of what you find.

chats.title: Open review platform with image screening

messages.text: Thinking about open review again. If a preprint server let anyone post structured public comments, would that improve papers, or would only a handful of preprints ever get meaningful attention? I want to understand what makes post-publication review on preprints actually useful rather than just a comment box nobody reads.

Evidence suggests open comment sections get used rarely unless something structures participation. Things that help include invited reviewers who publish their reports openly, community review groups that pick preprints to evaluate, short structured forms rather than free text, and author responses displayed alongside comments. Visibility also matters; if comments are surfaced next to the preprint and linked from the published version, authors have more incentive to engage.

Structured and invited review makes sense. Here's where I could contribute something concrete: my image duplication detector could run automatically on every new preprint, and its flags could be shown to reviewers as a prompt to look closer. It's a tool I built and already share with other groups, so integrating it wouldn't be much work.

Automated screening could give open reviewers a useful starting point, especially for biology preprints with lots of figures. I'd recommend not publicly displaying raw flags, since false positives could damage reputations unfairly. Instead, flags could go privately to invited reviewers or server moderators, who then decide whether to raise the issue. Clear documentation of what the detector checks would help reviewers interpret its output.

Yes, private flags only, that's important. I'd also want to evaluate whether this combination actually improves the published versions: preprints with structured open review plus image screening versus preprints without. That's the question I keep coming back to, whether public review changes the final paper at all.

A comparison like that would directly address your recurring question. You could track concrete outcomes such as figure corrections, changes to conclusions, and added analyses between preprint and published versions. Randomizing which preprints receive invited open review, if a server is willing, would make the comparison much stronger than an observational one. Even a small pilot with one willing server would provide useful preliminary data.

My citation analysis is mostly done and the bias toward positive results holds up after adjusting for venue and year. Now I'm trying to write the discussion. I want to argue that citation bias doesn't exist in isolation; it's reinforced by how researchers are evaluated. What are the standard arguments linking citation patterns to incentive structures?

Common arguments include that citations feed into metrics used for evaluation, so researchers prefer producing findings likely to be cited, which tend to be novel and positive. Journals, which care about their own citation rates, favor such papers, creating a loop. Null results are less likely to be written up at all, the file drawer problem, so the literature that can be cited is already skewed. Your discussion could position citation bias as both a symptom and a reinforcer of these incentives.

The loop framing helps. The piece I want to add is about hiring committees. My sense is that when committees lean heavily on paper counts, it pushes people toward slicing work into many small publishable units and chasing positive results, because a null result often doesn't become a paper at all. I'd like to discuss that as a system-level incentive, not about any particular department.

That's a well-recognized concern. Reliance on publication counts rewards quantity and speed, encourages salami slicing, and penalizes long or risky projects that may end in nulls. Some evaluation reforms propose limiting candidates to a few selected outputs with narrative descriptions of contribution, or explicitly valuing data sharing, replications and null results. Linking this to your citation findings would show how evaluation practices at the hiring stage feed into the literature's skew.

Good, I'll keep it to one paragraph so the discussion doesn't drift away from my data. Something like: citation bias favors positive results, hiring by paper counts favors producing many positive papers, and the two reinforce each other. Then a sentence about evaluation reforms.

That paragraph structure is tight and well-supported. Be careful to label the hiring link as an interpretation rather than a finding, since your data don't directly measure hiring. A suggestion for future work, such as studying whether institutions that adopted narrative CVs see changes in null result publication, would end the discussion on a constructive, testable note. Keeping that line clear will make the argument more credible.
